frameworks.role: Defines the deprecation and disallowance TIMELINE. This is the source of the dates that make our reports actionable.

Finite Field DH and MQV, Elliptic Curve DH and MQV, RSA (key establishment)
Finite Field DH and MQV, Elliptic Curve DH and MQV, RSA (key establishment) — ALL sizes

keyDates.note: Verbatim: 'NIST has a few symmetric cryptography standards at the 112-bit security level, which will be disallowed in 2030.' IR 8547 does NOT enumerate which standards those are, so no algorithm entry in algorithms.json claims this row. Naming a specific algorithm here would be an over-claim; it needs a different primary source (SP 800-131A Rev 2 / SP 800-67) before it can attach to a finding.

frameworks.criticalNuance: Larger classical key sizes do NOT extend the deadline. RSA-3072 and P-384 are disallowed after 2035 on the same schedule as RSA-2048 and P-256. The only difference is that 112-bit parameters get an earlier DEPRECATION milestone in 2030. Many vendors get this wrong.
frameworks.contextQuote: §4.1.1: SP 800-57pt1 had projected NIST would disallow 112-bit public-key schemes on 2031-01-01; IR 8547 instead DEPRECATES them at that level so organisations can continue use while migrating.

applicationSpecificGuidance.note: §4.2 is the reason the 2035 date must never be presented as a target. C4's `ir8547-2035-is-a-ceiling` and `ir8547-key-establishment-priority` obligations below are built from these two quotes and nothing else.
quotes: §4.2: 'While NIST's cryptographic algorithm standards may continue to specify quantum-vulnerable techniques until 2035 and generally allow their use, these application-specific standards and guidelines may specify earlier transitions for certain cryptographic algorithms, techniques, and protocols used within these applications.'

§4.2: 'NIST expects to prioritize the migration to quantum-resistant key-establishment schemes within these updates to protect against "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks, particularly in interactive protocols like TLS and IKE.'

§4.1.2: 'in order to mitigate the risk of "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks on network communications, application-specific guidance, as described in Sec. 4.2, may require or recommend migration to quantum-resistant key establishment schemes before the classical schemes are generally disallowed.'

hybridAndDualSignatures.note: §3.2 — what an organisation is ALLOWED to do while migrating. Recorded because a report that only states prohibitions gives no migration path.
quotes: §3.2.1: 'NIST currently allows a generic composite key-establishment technique described in SP 800-56C ... any shared secret key generated as specified in FIPS 203 may be used as the value Z in the generic composite mode described in SP 800-56C.'
§3.2.2: 'Existing NIST standards and guidelines accommodate their use provided that at least one component digital signature algorithm is NIST-approved.'
§3.2.2: 'NIST will accommodate the use of a hybrid key-establishment mode and dual signatures in FIPS 140 validation when suitably combined with a NIST-approved scheme.'

frameworks.retrievalNote: PDF downloaded from nvlpubs.nist.gov and read in full on 2026-08-16 (Tables 1–7, §3.2, §4, §4.1.1–4.1.3, §4.2). Every date and quote in this entry was re-read against that copy; none changed from the 2026-08-01 reading.
frameworks.customerFacingRule: Because this is a DRAFT, every customer-facing use must be labelled 'NIST draft guidance (IR 8547 ipd, November 2024)'. Presenting these as final binding dates is a factual error.

findingObligations.requirement: Do not treat 2035 as the migration target for this algorithm. NIST states that application-specific standards and guidelines may specify earlier transitions than the general algorithm-standard dates, so the binding date for a given system may be earlier than the table date.
findingObligations.deadlineNote: IR 8547 §4.2: 'While NIST's cryptographic algorithm standards may continue to specify quantum-vulnerable techniques until 2035 and generally allow their use, these application-specific standards and guidelines may specify earlier transitions for certain cryptographic algorithms, techniques, and protocols used within these applications.'

findingObligations.requirement: Migrate this key-establishment use ahead of the general timeline. NIST expects to prioritise migration to quantum-resistant key establishment in its application-specific guidance to protect against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks, particularly in interactive protocols like TLS and IKE.
findingObligations.deadlineNote: IR 8547 §4.1.2: application-specific guidance 'may require or recommend migration to quantum-resistant key establishment schemes before the classical schemes are generally disallowed.' The 2030/2035 rows are therefore a ceiling for this purpose, not a schedule.

findingObligations.requirement: A hybrid construction is an approved migration path for this algorithm: a composite key-establishment mode per SP 800-56C, or a dual signature, is accommodated by existing NIST standards provided at least one component is NIST-approved.
findingObligations.caveat: IR 8547 §3.2.2: 'NIST leaves the decision to each specific application as to whether it can afford the implementation cost, performance reduction, and engineering complexity ... of a hybrid mode for key establishment or the use of dual signatures.' This is an allowance, not a recommendation, and hybrid mode does not by itself satisfy the 2030/2035 transition rows.

frameworks.notClaimed: IR 8547 Table 7 records SHA-1 at 80 bits of collision security (Category <1) and SHA-224/SHA-512/224/SHA3-224 at 112 bits. Those are security-strength statements, NOT transition rules, and IR 8547 attaches no date to any of them — so no IR 8547 deadline or obligation is derived for a hash entry here. SHA-1's rules stay sourced to SP 800-131A Rev 2 §9, where they actually live.

frameworks.name: Digital Signature Standard (DSS)
frameworks.role: Defines the approved digital signature algorithms. Withdrew DSA for signature generation — a PRESENT-TENSE obligation with no migration runway, independent of any quantum timeline. Referenced by `algorithms.json`'s `dsa` deadlines; the id matches that `framework` string exactly.

frameworks.name: Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths
frameworks.role: In-force (non-draft) transition rules for classical algorithms. §9's SHA-1 rules are USE-DEPENDENT — the same algorithm is disallowed, legacy-allowed or acceptable depending on what it is used for. Referenced by `algorithms.json`'s `sha1` deadlines; the id matches that `framework` string exactly.

frameworks.name: Secure Hash Standard (SHS)
frameworks.role: Enumerates the approved hash functions. An absent hash (MD5) was never approved, so no transition schedule exists and none may be cited. Referenced by `algorithms.json`'s `md5` deadlines; the id matches that `framework` string exactly.

frameworks.name: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation
frameworks.role: Defines ECB as one of five APPROVED confidentiality modes. This entry exists so nothing in the product can present AES-ECB as a NIST violation: the correct framing is a best-practice finding (no semantic security), and the auditor-checkable citation is this document, NOT SP 800-38D. See open gap G-09.

documents: SP 1800-38A — Executive Summary (preliminary draft, comment closed 2023-06-08)
SP 1800-38B — Approach, Architecture, and Security Characteristics of Public Key Application Discovery Tools (preliminary draft, December 2023)
SP 1800-38C — Quantum Readiness: Testing Draft Standards for Interoperability and Performance (preliminary draft, December 2023)
frameworks.status: PRELIMINARY DRAFT — Volumes B and C comment period closed 2024-02-20. Additional volumes expected.
frameworks.role: THE MOST DIRECTLY RELEVANT NIST PUBLICATION TO THIS PRODUCT. Volume B is a practice guide for cryptographic discovery TOOLS — i.e. the exact product category QuantaXscan is in. It defines a discovery architecture, a normalisation scheme for discovery output, and a functional test plan for evaluating discovery tools.
frameworks.whyItMatters: IR 8547 tells us WHICH algorithms must go and by when. The CISA factsheet tells us inventory comes first. SP 1800-38B tells us HOW a discovery tool should be built and what it should emit. It is the closest thing to a specification for our product, and a buyer evaluating us may well use its functional test plan (Appendix C, eight use cases) as an evaluation rubric.

discoveryArchitecture.note: SP 1800-38B §4.1 defines three discovery domains. Our collector roadmap should map onto these explicitly.

domains.name: Protecting the Code Development Pipeline
domains.covers: CI/CD pipeline software, SDLC software, repository components

domains.name: Operational Systems and Applications
domains.covers: Filesystem scanning sensors on end-user devices and servers; EDR integration; BINARY scanning for third-party code with no available source
ourCollectors: B10 binaries — NOTE: NIST treats binary scanning as core, not deferred

domains.name: Transport Protocols and Network Services
domains.covers: Real-time network scanning and passive discovery from historical packet captures, across cloud, on-premises and untrusted networks

discoveryModalities.note: SP 1800-38B §4.1.4 names four ways discovery data is obtained. Our confidence model should distinguish them.

normalisationRequirement.note: DIRECT VALIDATION of our collector/observation design — and a concrete schema requirement we do not currently meet.
normalisationRequirement.problemQuote: §4.1.4: 'The reports produced by the discovery platforms in this demonstration are unique in that they do not use a common format for representing the discovery results. In a contrived example, a network discovery platform may identify a host system as host.example.com:443, whereas another may omit the port number (host.example.com). Therefore, we identified the need for a common format to represent normalized discovery reports, ideally by leveraging existing normalization efforts to the extent possible.'
normalisationRequirement.scopeNote: §4.1.4 explicitly states it 'does not define a schema, but instead defines descriptive data elements'. So this is guidance to align with, not a format to serialise to — CycloneDX CBOM remains our wire format.

networkDataElements.representation: String — IANA Service Name or TLS ALPN ID (RFC 6335 §5.1 / RFC 7301)
String — Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) 2.3, NIST IR 7695

normalisationRequirement.actionRequired: Our asset model uses a freeform jsonb locationDetail. To align, network-surface assets should carry these named elements with CPE 2.3 for software/OS/vendor identification. See open gap G-15.

consortiumMembers.note: COMMERCIAL REALITY CHECK. SP 1800-38B §5.1 lists the technology collaborators who contributed discovery tools to the NCCoE lab. These are the credible competitors in this exact category — not a spreadsheet.

frameworks.functionalTestPlan: Appendix C defines eight use cases for a Discovery Platform Lab Functional Demonstration. Worth treating as an acceptance-test suite for our own collectors, and as a likely buyer evaluation rubric.

frameworks.tlp: TLP:CLEAR — may be shared without restriction
frameworks.role: The authoritative statement that quantum readiness begins with a cryptographic inventory. The structure our dashboard mirrors.
frameworks.CORRECTION: This document does NOT define a numbered five-stage roadmap. Earlier seed data in this repo invented one. The factsheet is organised into the NAMED SECTIONS listed below. Do not present numbered stages as quoted from CISA.

sections.heading: DISCUSS POST-QUANTUM ROADMAPS WITH TECHNOLOGY VENDORS

discoveryTargets.note: Under PREPARE A CRYPTOGRAPHIC INVENTORY, the factsheet names exactly three places cryptographic discovery tools should look. Our collector roadmap should map onto these explicitly.
targets: Network protocols, used to identify quantum-vulnerable algorithms in network protocols that allow traceability
Assets on end user systems and servers, including applications and associated libraries, both within application functionality and for firmware and software updates
Cryptographic code or dependencies in the continuous integration/continuous delivery development pipeline
discoveryTargets.embeddedCryptoWarning: Quoted: 'Discovery tools may not be able to identify embedded cryptography used internally within products, hindering discoverability or documentation. Organizations should ask vendors for lists of embedded cryptography within their products.' — PRIMARY-SOURCE SUPPORT for our coverage-gap panel (feature D3). CISA itself says tools have blind spots.

dataLifetimeSupport.note: PRIMARY-SOURCE SUPPORT for the X variable in Mosca (feature A3). CORRECTED 2026-08-16: these three quotes were listed as though they shared one section. They do not — they come from three different named sections, and a citation that says otherwise is wrong in the one way an auditor can check. Each quote now carries the heading it actually appears under.

quotes.quote: 'cyber threat actors could be targeting data today that would still require protection in the future (or in other words, has a long secrecy lifetime), using a catch now, break later or harvest now, decrypt later operation'

'Organizations should include in their inventory when and where quantum-vulnerable cryptography is being leveraged to protect the most sensitive and critical datasets and include estimates on length of protection for these datasets.'
'Prioritization should be given to high impact systems, industrial control systems (ICSs), and systems with long-term confidentiality/secrecy needs.'

roadmapAlignment.note: C6. What the product does against each of the factsheet's own named sections — not a numbered stage model, which this document does not have (see CORRECTION). `productRole` is deliberately three-valued so that 'we evidence this' is never printed as 'we do this'.

sections.heading: WHY PREPARE NOW?
sections.note: The harvest-now-decrypt-later argument is what the A3 secrecy-lifetime input and the Mosca inequality express. The product supplies the exposure evidence; the urgency judgement is the customer's.

sections.heading: ESTABLISH A QUANTUM-READINESS ROADMAP
sections.note: Establishing a project team and a roadmap is customer process. The product supplies the inventory that section says the roadmap must start from, and nothing more. Claiming to produce the roadmap would be an over-claim.

sections.heading: PREPARE A CRYPTOGRAPHIC INVENTORY
sections.note: This is the section QuantaXscan automates. The three discovery targets named under it map to the collector surfaces — see `discoveryTargets`. The factsheet's own embedded-cryptography warning is why a coverage-gap panel (D3) is required rather than optional.

sections.heading: DISCUSS POST-QUANTUM ROADMAPS WITH TECHNOLOGY VENDORS
sections.note: The vendor assessment register (B9) records what vendors answered. The product does not conduct the engagement.

sections.heading: SUPPLY CHAIN QUANTUM-READINESS
sections.note: Dependency and vendor findings show where the reliance is. Prioritisation of high-impact systems and ICS is a customer risk decision the product informs.

sections.heading: TECHNOLOGY VENDOR RESPONSIBILITIES
sections.note: Addressed to vendors, not to the organisation being scanned. No product claim.

FIPS 203, 204 and 205 were finalised in August 2024. The factsheet's PROCESS guidance (inventory first, prioritise by secrecy lifetime, engage vendors) is what this entry is cited for and it is unaffected; its draft-standards language must never be surfaced as current. No superseding revision was found on 2026-08-16.

frameworks.secondarySourceConflict: Checked again on 2026-08-16 and this is why the dates below stay `needs-check` rather than being promoted. qDayNote: These are REGULATORY deadlines, not predictions of when a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer will exist. That framing is both more defensible and more useful — compliance dates bind long before the physics does. The UI must say this explicitly rather than implying we know when Q-Day is. Note the 2030 and 2035 figures now trace to a verified primary source (IR 8547 ipd), but that source is a DRAFT.
